why_how.text: Match speed to conditions, share the road courteously, and move only when safe and clear of traffic.
Walk around a parked car before reversing, and never reverse or halt in a travel lane; keep going to a safe pull-off.
Obey officers, flaggers, traffic devices and traffic laws as the first rule of the road.
Signal one hundred feet before turning in town and three hundred feet before turning on rural roads.
Keep right except to pass on roads with three or more same-direction lanes, favoring the center lane amid entering traffic.
After a missed turn or forgotten signal, continue to the next intersection, get in position, signal, then turn.
Never drive on the shoulder unless directed to do so.
Obey posted limits and drop below them for bad road or weather conditions.
Interstates post seventy-five or eighty for cars and light trucks by day and night, with heavy trucks held to sixty-five.
Urban-area highways post sixty-five for all listed vehicles day and night near Billings, Great Falls and Missoula.
Two-lane highways post seventy by day and sixty-five at night for cars and light trucks, with heavy trucks at sixty days and fifty-five nights.
A two-lane driver may exceed the limit by ten miles per hour while overtaking and returning safely right.
Pass only when safe, using the left of the centerline on two-lane roads and the leftmost lane on multi-lane roads.
Passing on the right is legal only past a left-turning vehicle or on wide multi-lane pavement, never off the roadway or on the shoulder.
Without turn controls, turn from the lane nearest the destination side into the nearest lane of the new road.
Keep right turns tight without swinging wide left first or finishing wide in the far lane.
Avoid cutting left turns into approaching traffic while leaving room for oncoming left-turning vehicles.
Turn around only with five hundred feet of clear view both ways and no approaching vehicles, never on busy streets, curves or hills.
No turn is made unless the vehicle is in the proper lane and the move is safe.
The law assigns yielding duty and grants no absolute right-of-way, so every driver must act to avoid striking anyone.
Blind pedestrians with a guide dog or white cane hold absolute right-of-way; never sound the horn at them.
Drivers yield to pedestrians in crosswalks, yet no pedestrian may step off the curb into a vehicle path.
Night walkers should wear light clothing or carry a light, and walking on the roadway is unlawful where sidewalks exist.
Roadway walkers keep left facing traffic, cross at intersections using provided crosswalks, and obey applicable traffic laws.
Passing left of the centerline is the two-lane norm, while passing on the right is limited to left-turning vehicles and wide multi-lane pavement.
Right-of-way is yielded under the rules, never seized, and every driver must still act to avoid a crash.
Town turns need a one-hundred-foot signal and rural turns a three-hundred-foot signal, with the shoulder never a driving lane.

title.text: Right of way and school buses

why_how.text: Drivers crossing sidewalks or entering and leaving driveways, alleys and lots yield to pedestrians; sidewalk driving is illegal except to cross.
Left-turning drivers yield to oncoming through traffic, and circle entrants yield to traffic already circulating.
At uncontrolled intersections yield to the vehicle on the right, staying ready to yield by covering the brake and scanning both ways.
At a four-way stop the first arrival goes first after a full stop; driveway and roadside entrants stop and yield to main-road traffic.
Never enter an intersection without room to clear it, and treat a yield sign as an order to slow and yield to all vehicles.
Right on red is allowed after stopping in the proper lane when safe unless signed otherwise, as is left on red between one-way streets.
Yield to pedestrians in crosswalks; a stopped driver turns right only when the pedestrian is in the opposite half and safe.
Drivers behind a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian must not pass the stopped vehicle.
An overtaking driver yields to the vehicle being passed even as it slows or stops.
Yield to siren-and-light emergency vehicles by pulling as far right as possible, obeying loudspeaker orders, and staying stopped until they pass.
Stop at least thirty feet from a red-flashing school bus from either direction until the lights end, slowing with care for slowing or yellow-flashing buses.
An uncontrolled intersection yields to the vehicle on the right, while a four-way stop releases the first arrival after a full stop.
A stopped driver turns right only with the pedestrian in the opposite half and safe, while following drivers must never pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian.

A funeral procession means two or more vehicles with lead and escort units, one carrying remains, traveling in daylight hours.
Outsiders yield to procession vehicles and must not split, join for advantage, pass on the right, or cross its path through red.
The lead vehicle obeys intersection controls, after which followers may proceed through with reasonable care for others.
Procession drivers follow closely, cap speed at fifty-five on fast highways and near the limit elsewhere, burn all lights, and flash signals together on first and last cars.
Procession drivers still yield to signaled emergency vehicles and keep due regard for every road user.
Bicycles count as vehicles under the traffic laws that reasonably fit, so motorists adjust for their slower travel when passing and sharing.
Pass a cyclist as a slow vehicle by crossing the centerline with no oncoming traffic to leave a recommended five feet, or by slowing to the cyclist pace until passing is safe.
Expect cyclists off the shoulder and often in single-file groups that need extra passing time.
Cyclists ride as far right as practical, often eighteen to twenty-four inches into the lane to deter unsafe in-lane passes.
Shared-lane arrow markings guide cyclist position and warn motorists to leave room, differing from bike-lane bicycle symbols.
Motorists grant cyclists full vehicle rights, never deliberately block them, pass only without endangering anyone, and yield inside designated bike lanes.
Cyclists ride single file except on exclusive paths, when passing another bike, two abreast on shoulders or parking lanes, or two abreast on multi-lane roads without extra impedance.
Slower-than-traffic cyclists keep near the right edge except when passing, preparing a left turn, dodging hazards or narrow lanes, or avoiding parked-car doors.
Bicycles often lack mirrors, so drivers treat an approached cyclist as unaware and proceed with extra care.
